::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives

- Split a long Snakefile into rule files with `include:`, with shared code in `common.smk`.
- Add a config switch that turns a part of the pipeline on or off, and predict how the job list changes.
- Choose between `shell:`, `run:` and `script:`, and read rule inputs from Python and R scripts.
- Use `onstart`, `onsuccess` and `onerror` to report on a run.

Time: 50 min
:::

## From one file to many

At stopping point B, RegPipe was one `Snakefile` of about 300 lines. That works
until two people edit it in the same week. The lab pipelines all split it the
same way:

```
workflows/
  RegPipe.snakefile        # config, hooks, rule all, include: lines
  rules/
    common.smk             # samplesheet, paths, switches, helper functions
    align.smk              # fastqc, bowtie2_index, align, filter
    peaks.smk              # call_peaks, consensus_peaks
    tracks.smk             # bigwig, locus_plot
    report.smk             # frip, qc_table, ctcf_rad21_overlap, enhancer_activity
```

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
Nothing about the rules changes when you split them. Snakemake reads the
included files as if their text were pasted at the `include:` line. The
point is that a person looking for the peak caller opens `peaks.smk` and finds
it, and a diff of a pull request touches one small file. The field guide's
[Lab layout](../field-guide/conventions.qmd#layouts) section compares this
with the community's `workflow/Snakefile` layout.
:::

## `include:`

The main file is short. It loads the config, includes `common.smk` first,
declares the hooks and `rule all`, then includes the rule files:

{{< snippet repo="regpipe" file="workflows/RegPipe.snakefile" lines="15-39" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
Order matters in two places:

- `common.smk` must come before any rule file, because the rules use its
  names (`OUT`, `LOGS`, `fastq`, `filtered_bam`, ...). Python reads top to
  bottom; a name that is not defined yet is an error at parse time.
- `rules.bowtie2_index.output` (in `align`) only works if `bowtie2_index` was
  defined earlier. Both rules are in `align.smk`, so the order inside that
  file takes care of it.

Paths in `include:` are relative to the file that contains the line, so
`"rules/align.smk"` means `workflows/rules/align.smk`. The same is true for
`script:` paths. RegPipe builds them from `workflow.basedir` (the folder of
the main Snakefile) to make that explicit:

{{< snippet repo="regpipe" file="workflows/rules/common.smk" lines="24-27" >}}
:::

::: {.notes}
`configfile:` loads the default config. When the launcher passes
`--configfile`, Snakemake 8 merges that file on top, key by key. That is why a
small YAML with only the keys you change works (exercise 6.4).
:::

## `common.smk` holds what every rule needs

Read the samplesheet once, name the outputs once, and every rule file uses the
same names. One helper per kind of output keeps `rule all` and the rules in
step:

{{< snippet repo="regpipe" file="workflows/rules/common.smk" lines="109-123" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
If `call_peaks` writes `peak_file(s)` and `rule all` asks for `peak_file(s)`,
a change of folder in one place cannot break the other. Module 3 built the
samplesheet parsing; it moved here unchanged.
:::

## Switches

Some parts of RegPipe are optional. The locus figure needs R and plotgardener,
which has no Apple-silicon build. The TT-seq tables need files from GEO. Each is
a switch in `config/RegConfig.yaml`:

```yaml
make_locus_plot: true
ttseq:
  enabled: true
```

`common.smk` turns them into Python booleans, once:

{{< snippet repo="regpipe" file="workflows/rules/common.smk" lines="79-81" >}}

{{< snippet repo="regpipe" file="workflows/rules/common.smk" lines="90-91" >}}

## A switch does two things

First, it decides what `rule all` asks for. This is a target function:

{{< snippet repo="regpipe" file="workflows/rules/common.smk" def="all_targets" >}}

Second, it can decide whether a rule exists at all:

{{< snippet repo="regpipe" file="workflows/rules/report.smk" lines="72-77" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
The first is enough to keep a job out of the run: if nothing asks for
`enhancer_activity.tsv`, Snakemake never schedules the rule. The second goes
further. With `ttseq.enabled: false`, `TTSEQ` has no `bigwigs` and
`TTSEQ_TRACKS` is empty, so the rule's inputs would not even make sense.
Defining it under `if` means Snakemake never sees it. `locus_plot` is defined
under `if MAKE_LOCUS_PLOT:` for the same reason.
:::

## TTpipe does the same, bigger

TTpipe has more switches (`run_processing`, `run_analysis`, `trim`,
`spike_in.enabled`, ...). Its target function reads like a table of contents:

{{< snippet repo="ttpipe" file="workflows/rules/common.smk" def="all_targets" >}}

and a whole rule file can be switched:

{{< snippet repo="ttpipe" file="workflows/TTpipe.snakefile" lines="52-59" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
Most of `processing.smk` sits under `if RUN_PROCESSING:`, so an analysis-only
run on an existing count matrix has no alignment rules at all. The field guide
walks through all of TTpipe's switches in
[Switches](../field-guide/ttpipe.qmd#tt-switches) and
[Rules defined under `if`](../field-guide/ttpipe.qmd#tt-conditional-rules).
:::

Add `run_fastqc: true` to the config. When it is `false`, no `fastqc` job
should run. Change only `common.smk` and the config. How many jobs does the dry
run list with the switch on, and with it off?

## Switching from the command line

You can flip a top-level switch for one run with `--config`. Watch the case:

{{< generated name="regpipe-config-false" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
Snakemake 8.27.1 turns `True` and `False` into booleans, but leaves `false` as
the text `"false"`. `bool("false")` is `True` in Python, so the plot stays in,
and nothing warns you. The same thing happens inside nested values:
`--config 'ttseq={"enabled": false}'` sets `enabled` to the text `"false"`.

For anything nested, write a small YAML file with only the keys you change and
pass it with `--configfile`. Snakemake merges it into the default config:

```bash
printf 'ttseq:\n  enabled: false\n' > no_ttseq.yaml
snakemake -n -s workflows/RegPipe.snakefile --cores 1 --configfile no_ttseq.yaml
```

For a run through the launcher, copy `config/RegConfig.yaml`, edit the copy,
and pass the whole file: `bash RegPipe.sh --configfile config/no_ttseq.yaml`.
The launcher reads `hpcProfile` and `outputDir` from the file you give it.
:::

::: {.notes}
This one bites people. Run the two commands live if there is time.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .exercise}

## `shell:`, `run:` and `script:`

A rule's action can take three forms.

| | Runs | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| `shell:` | a bash command, in the rule's conda env | any command-line tool |
| `run:` | Python, inside the Snakemake process itself | a few lines that need the samplesheet or config |
| `script:` | a `.py` or `.R` file, in the rule's conda env | anything longer than a few lines, and all R |

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
`run:` code runs in the same Python that runs Snakemake. It can see every
variable in the Snakefile, which is handy, but it cannot use a `conda:` env,
cannot be tested on its own, and `snakemake --lint` flags long `run:` blocks.
`script:` code runs in the rule's environment, gets everything it needs from a
`snakemake` object, and is an ordinary file you can open in your editor.
:::

## `run:` in TTpipe

TTpipe's only `run:` block writes the sample table for DESeq2:

{{< snippet repo="ttpipe" file="workflows/TTpipe.snakefile" rule="sample_table" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
Read the comment above the rule. The samplesheet is listed as an **input**.
The table is built from Snakemake's parsed copy of the samplesheet, so the
file is not needed to make it. It is there so that editing the samplesheet
makes the table out of date. Without it, a run after adding samples kept the
old table, and DESeq2 failed because the sample names did not match the count
matrix. That happened on a real run. If a rule's output depends on a file,
make the file an input, even if the rule never opens it. The field guide has
the full story in [Samplesheet as input](../field-guide/ttpipe.qmd#tt-sample-table).
:::

## `script:` in Python

RegPipe's `frip` rule hands its files to a Python script:

{{< snippet repo="regpipe" file="workflows/rules/report.smk" rule="frip" >}}

Inside the script, the rule's directives are attributes of `snakemake`:

{{< snippet repo="regpipe" file="scripts/frip.py" lines="36-57" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
`snakemake.input.bam`, `snakemake.output.tsv`, `snakemake.wildcards.sample`,
`snakemake.log[0]`: the names are the ones in the rule. There are no
command-line arguments to parse. The script needs `pysam`, which is in
`envs/regpipe_peaks.yml`, the rule's `conda:` env.
:::

## `script:` in R

R gets an S4 object, so you use `@` and `$`:

{{< snippet repo="regpipe" file="scripts/locus_plot.R" lines="33-46" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
`snakemake@input$bigwigs` is a list, one entry per file, in the order the rule
listed them. The rule also passes parallel lists in `params:` (sample names,
their targets) so the script can match them up. The lab's R style applies
here as anywhere: the native pipe `|>`, and Bioconductor (`rtracklayer`,
`GenomicRanges`, `plotgardener`) for genomic data.
:::

## The venv-python trap

`script:` runs a `.py` file with the Python of the rule's conda env. If the rule
has no env, or you run without conda, it uses the Python that runs Snakemake.
For the launcher, that is the venv in `env/`, which has Snakemake and pandas
and nothing else:

```
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pysam'
```

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
We hit this while building RegPipe, running the `script:` rules without
`--use-conda`. The fix is not to install `pysam` into the venv. Give every
`script:` rule a `conda:` env that has what the script imports, and run with
the profile (which sets `software-deployment-method: conda`). This is the same
problem as the interpreter-line issue in [module 5](05-cluster.qmd), seen from
the other side: the venv's Python must never be the one that runs your
analysis code.
:::

## Hooks: `onstart`, `onsuccess`, `onerror`

Three blocks of Python that run once per run, on the machine where Snakemake
runs (your laptop, or the launcher job on the cluster):

{{< snippet repo="regpipe" file="workflows/RegPipe.snakefile" lines="21-30" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
`notify()` is in `common.smk`. It sends one email per event if an address is
set (`REGPIPE_EMAIL` in `~/.bashrc`, or `notify: email:` in the config), and it
never lets a failed email fail the run:

{{< snippet repo="regpipe" file="workflows/rules/common.smk" def="notify" >}}

Three things to know about hooks:

- They do not run in a dry run, or when there is nothing to do.
- `onerror` runs when a job fails. It does not run for a mistake in the
  Snakefile itself: that stops Snakemake before any hook is set up.
- `log` inside the hook is the path of Snakemake's own log for this run.

MicroCPipe, TTpipe and ChromSimPipe all have the same `notify()`. TTpipe's
`onerror` adds the last lines of the log to the email
([hooks](../field-guide/microcpipe.qmd#mc-hooks)).
:::

## Key points

- `include:` pastes a rule file in place. Include `common.smk` first; define a rule before another rule uses `rules.X`.
- Name each kind of output once, in a helper in `common.smk`, and use it in the rule and in `rule all`.
- A switch is a boolean in `common.smk`. It decides what the target function asks for, and it can put rules under `if` so they do not exist.
- On the command line, `--config key=False` with a capital F. For nested keys, use a small YAML file and `--configfile`.
- `shell:` for tools, `script:` for anything longer than a few lines and all R, `run:` only for a few lines. Every `script:` rule needs a `conda:` env.
- If a file changes what a rule writes, make it an input.
